title: The death of Adrian IV, the only English pope
shortBlurb: Nicholas Breakspear of Hertfordshire, the only Englishman ever to sit in Peter's chair, died at Anagni, and a disputed succession opened a long schism…
body: Nicholas Breakspear, born about 1100 at Abbots Langley near St. Albans in Hertfordshire, rose from the cloister of St. Rufus to be cardinal-bishop of Albano and the legate who ordered the Church in Scandinavia, erecting Nidaros as its archbishopric. On 4 December 1154 the cardinals chose him pope as Adrian IV, and no other Englishman has sat in Peter's chair since.

His five years were stormy. He crowned Frederick Barbarossa emperor in 1155, quarreled with him two years later at Besançon over the word 'benefice,' made peace with the Norman king of Sicily at Benevento, and, by the bull Laudabiliter — a document whose authenticity scholars still dispute — is said to have granted Henry II of England the lordship of Ireland. Rome itself, in the grip of the commune and of Arnold of Brescia, he could hardly hold, and he spent much of his pontificate away from it.

On 1 September 1159, at Anagni, he died suddenly; the chroniclers tell a strange tale of a fly caught in his throat, while later writers suppose a quinsy. Within days the double election of Alexander III and the antipope Victor IV split the Church in a schism of eighteen years, and Adrian was laid in St. Peter's, the one English pope.

title: Terror is declared the order of the day
shortBlurb: Pressed by the Paris sections, the National Convention made terror the order of the day, and the machinery of the guillotine turned upon the Church…
body: In the summer of 1793 the Republic stood besieged: royalist rebels held the Vendée, federalist revolts burned in the provinces, and the allied armies pressed the frontiers. On 5 September the Paris sections crowded into the National Convention demanding vengeance on the enemies within, and Bertrand Barère, for the Committee of Public Safety, gave the day its watchword: let terror be placed on the order of the day.

The Convention complied. The Law of Suspects followed on 17 September; the revolutionary calendar swept away the Christian week in October; and in November Notre-Dame itself was rededicated as a Temple of Reason. Across France refractory priests were herded to the guillotine or to the prison-hulks of Rochefort, and the Carmelite nuns of Compiègne would mount the scaffold the following July, singing.

By the reckoning of later historians some sixteen thousand official death sentences were pronounced before the fever broke with Robespierre's fall on 9 Thermidor (27 July 1794), and tens of thousands more perished without judgment. The Church that emerged from the Terror was stripped, scattered, and poorer in everything but its martyrs.

title: The battle of the Frigidus
shortBlurb: On the river Frigidus Theodosius broke the army of the usurper Eugenius, and with it the last armed hope of Roman paganism…
body: When Valentinian II died at Vienne in 392, the Frankish general Arbogast raised to the western throne his secretary Eugenius, a teacher of rhetoric, and with him the pagan party of the senate made its last restoration: the Altar of Victory returned to the curia, and the old gods rode once more with the standards.

Theodosius I marched from the East and met them in the Julian Alps, on the river Frigidus — the Vipava of our maps — on 5 and 6 September 394. The first day cost him dear, his Gothic vanguard falling in thousands; but on the second, the church historians relate, the Bora wind rose and blew into the faces of the westerners, turning their own missiles back upon them.

Eugenius was taken in his tent and beheaded; Arbogast fled to the mountains and two days later fell upon his sword. Theodosius, master now of a world momentarily undivided, died at Milan the following January, leaving the empire to his sons Arcadius and Honorius — and the Frigidus has stood ever since as the last battle fought in the names of the old gods.

title: The outrage at Anagni
shortBlurb: Agents of Philip the Fair seized Pope Boniface VIII in his own palace at Anagni, a wound from which the medieval papacy never wholly recovered…
body: The quarrel between Boniface VIII and Philip IV of France, kindled over the taxing of clergy, had risen through the bulls Clericis laicos and Ausculta fili to Unam Sanctam (18 November 1302), the boldest claim a pope ever made over kings. In the spring of 1303 Philip's council resolved to bring Boniface to judgment, and his minister Guillaume de Nogaret crossed the Alps to do it.

On 7 September 1303, with Sciarra Colonna and a band of hired horse, Nogaret broke into Anagni, the pope's own city, and surprised him in his palace — one day before the bull Super Petri solio, excommunicating the king, was to be published. The aged pope, robed and seated with the cross before him, offered his neck, in the words the sources give him; that Colonna struck him with a mailed hand, the chroniclers report and the historians repeat with caution.

The townsfolk rose on the third day and freed him, but the blow was mortal. Boniface died at Rome on 11 October, Dante gave the outrage a canto in the Purgatorio, and within six years Clement V had carried the papal residence to Avignon — the seventy years the Church would call its Babylonian captivity.

title: The colloquy of Poissy
shortBlurb: Catherine de' Medici gathered cardinals and Calvinist ministers at Poissy in the last great attempt to hold France together in one faith…
body: On 9 September 1561, in the refectory of the convent of Poissy, hard by the royal castle of Saint-Germain, the boy king Charles IX took his seat among six cardinals and some forty archbishops and bishops. His mother Catherine de' Medici, with the chancellor Michel de L'Hôpital, had summoned the colloquy to essay what politics had failed of: a peace between the Church and the Reformed.

Theodore Beza, come from Geneva with Peter Martyr Vermigli, spoke for the ministers, and the cardinal of Lorraine answered for the prelates, with Diego Laínez, general of the Jesuits, at his side. Beza's first oration held even his opponents, until he came to the Supper and confessed the body of Christ to be as far from the bread as heaven is from the earth — and the assembly broke in murmurs that were never stilled.

Sessions dragged into October, and a smaller conference afterward, but the Eucharist admitted no middle term. The Edict of January 1562 granted the Huguenots a measured toleration; within weeks the blood shed at Vassy opened the wars of religion that would trouble France for six and thirty years.

title: The Council of Agde
shortBlurb: Under the tolerance of an Arian king, Caesarius of Arles gathered the bishops of Visigothic Gaul in council at Agde…
body: In 506 the Visigoths ruled the South of Gaul from Toulouse, Arians governing a Catholic people. With the leave of King Alaric II, Caesarius, the young archbishop of Arles, summoned the bishops of the realm to Agde, a little port of the Mediterranean, and there, in the church of St. Andrew on 10 September, five and thirty of them sat down to order the life of the Church.

The council's canons, seven and forty as commonly reckoned, though the medieval collections transmit more, fixed the ages of holy orders — five and twenty for the deacon, thirty for the priest — confirmed the right of asylum at the altar, and bound the clergy to the discipline that Caesarius preached all his life. Passed almost whole into Gratian's Decretum, they became part of the common law of the medieval Church.

The kingdom whose tolerance had sheltered the synod did not long endure: the next year Clovis and the Franks broke Alaric at Vouillé, and Visigothic rule in Gaul shrank to a strip of coast. The canons of Agde outlived the kingdom that permitted them.

title: The founding of the abbey of Cluny
shortBlurb: William the Pious of Aquitaine gave his hunting ground at Cluny to the apostles Peter and Paul, founding the abbey that would leaven a century…
body: By a charter dated 11 September 910, William I, called the Pious, duke of Aquitaine and count of Auvergne, gave his villa of Cluny in the Mâconnais 'to the Apostles Peter and Paul,' that a regular monastery might rise there under Berno, abbot of Baume. The legend loves to tell that the duke grudged his hunting ground, and that Berno answered: drive out the dogs, and put monks in their place.

The charter's genius lay in its freedom: the new house was to answer to no bishop and no lord, but to the Holy See alone, holding its lands of the apostles. Under a line of great abbots — Odo, Odilo, Hugh, and Peter the Venerable — that liberty drew well over a thousand priories into the congregation of Cluny, and its abbey church, consecrated in 1095, stood for centuries as the largest in Christendom.

Cluny's observance leavened the reform of the eleventh century, and its cloister gave the Church popes, among them Urban II. Suppressed in 1790, the great church was sold and razed in the years of the Revolution; a single transept survives to measure what was lost.

title: The death of Philip II of Spain
shortBlurb: The most Catholic king died among the Hieronymites of the Escorial, closing the proudest and most burdensome reign of the Spanish century…
body: On 13 September 1598 Philip II of Spain died at San Lorenzo de El Escorial, the palace-monastery he had built in the foothills of the Guadarrama, aged seventy-one, after an illness of fifty-two days borne, the witnesses agree, with terrible patience. He had been king of Spain since 1556, of Naples and Sicily since 1554, of Portugal since 1580, and, by his marriage to Mary Tudor, king-consort of England.

Under him the monarchy touched its zenith and spent itself. His half-brother Don John broke the Turk at Lepanto in 1571; the revolt of the Netherlands outlasted all his generals; the Armada he sent against England in 1588 came home in wreckage; and the royal treasury was declared bankrupt again and again. Through it all he governed as the first servant of the altars — the champion, in the words of the historians, of the Catholic Counter-Reformation.

He was buried the next day beneath the high altar of his basilica, and the crown passed to Philip III. The empire on which the sun never set, as his age first said of it, would spend the following century spending what he had gathered.

title: The election of Pope Urban VII
shortBlurb: Giovanni Battista Castagna was chosen pope as Urban VII and was dead of malaria before his coronation — the shortest pontificate on record…
body: Sixtus V died on 27 August 1590, and on 15 September the cardinals, swayed by the Spanish faction, elected Giovanni Battista Castagna, who took the name Urban VII. He was a Roman of a Genoese house, sixty-nine years old, a doctor of laws of Bologna who had served the Curia as Referendary of the Signatura, archbishop of Rossano, and Inquisitor General of the Roman Inquisition, and he had been cardinal these seven years.

He was already sick when elected. The malaria of the Roman summer was on him, and on 27 September, twelve days after his election and before he could be crowned, he died toward midnight. His is the shortest pontificate the Church remembers.

He was buried in St. Peter's, whence his remains were later carried to Santa Maria sopra Minerva. The cardinals returned to the Sistine Chapel and in December chose Gregory XIV; the year had seen three men bear the name of pope.

title: The death of Pope St. Martin I in exile
shortBlurb: Martin I, who would not bend to the emperor's Typos, died an exile at Cherson, the last pope the Church reckons a martyr…
body: Martin I, a Tuscan of Todi, had served as apocrisiarius at Constantinople before the clergy and people of Rome made him pope in July 649 — without waiting, in defiance of custom, for the emperor's mandate. That October he gathered one hundred and five bishops in the Lateran, and in twenty canons they condemned the Monothelite doctrine and the Typos of the Emperor Constans II.

The emperor's answer came slowly but surely. In June 653 the exarch's men arrested the pope in the Lateran basilica itself and shipped him to Constantinople, where a tribunal condemned him for treason; he was stripped of his pallium, flogged in public, and banished to Cherson in the Crimea.

There, on 16 September 655, he died of want and of his wounds, his letters from exile breathing still a dry irony over the price of bread. East and West together venerate him as the last martyr-pope; the doctrine for which he suffered, two wills in the one Christ, was defined at the Sixth Ecumenical Council a generation later, and his companion in confession, St. Maximus, bore the same witness with his own maimed body.

title: The battle of Chrysopolis
shortBlurb: Constantine's final victory over Licinius on the Bosporus made him master of the whole Roman world — and cleared the road to Nicaea…
body: For a decade after the Edict of Milan (313) the uneasy partnership of Constantine and Licinius wore down to war. Beaten at Adrianople in July 324 and stripped of his fleet in the Hellespont, Licinius abandoned Byzantium and made his last stand on the Asian shore, at Chrysopolis, beneath Chalcedon.

There, on 18 September 324, Constantine broke him. Eusebius, who wrote within living memory, sets the two camps in a parable: the labarum and the ministers of God with the one, Egyptian diviners and soothsayers with the other. The defeated left some five and twenty thousand on the field by the earliest reckoning; Licinius fled to Nicomedia and there surrendered, spared at the prayer of his wife Constantia, the victor's sister — and put to death the next year on a charge of conspiracy.

Constantine stood at last sole Augustus, and the Church entered a new world. Within the year he summoned the bishops to Nicaea; within six he refounded Byzantium as his city, dedicated in 330, on the very strait where the last battle had been won.

title: The death of the Emperor Charles V
shortBlurb: The emperor who had heard Luther at Worms and seen Trent open died, his crowns resigned, among the friars of Yuste…
body: Charles V, born at Ghent in 1500, lord of lands on which the sun never set, had spent forty years holding together an empire that no man could govern whole: before him Luther at the Diet of Worms in 1521, his unpaid army sacking Rome in 1527, the Protestants heard at Augsburg in 1530, broken at Mühlberg in 1547, and at last conceded a legal peace in 1555.

Weary and gout-ridden, he laid down his crowns one by one — the Netherlands and Spain to his son Philip in 1555 and 1556, the imperial title to his brother Ferdinand, accepted by the electors in February 1558 — and withdrew to the apartments he had prepared beside the Hieronymite monastery of San Jerónimo de Yuste, in the oak-woods of Extremadura.

There, on 21 September 1558, he died, aged fifty-eight, of a malarial fever, amid his books and his Titians, prepared by the friars for his passage; tradition adds that he held to the last a crucifix that had been his mother's. The last emperor crowned by a pope sleeps now in the Escorial, and his two inheritances, Spanish and Austrian, went their separate ways for three hundred years.

title: The death of Pope Clement XIV
shortBlurb: Ganganelli, the Franciscan pope whom the Bourbon courts pressed to destroy the Jesuits, died at Rome amid rumors the evidence has never sustained…
body: Giovanni Vincenzo Antonio Ganganelli, born at Santarcangelo near Rimini in 1705, a Conventual Franciscan named in religion Lorenzo, rose by learning and modesty to the cardinalate in 1759 and, in May 1769, to the tiara as Clement XIV — chosen after a conclave in which the ambassadors of France and Spain had labored openly.

Those courts, with Naples and Portugal behind them, demanded one thing: the extinction of the Society of Jesus. After four years of resistance and delay, on 21 July 1773, Clement signed the brief Dominus ac Redemptor, suppressing the Society for the peace of the Church throughout the world.

He outlived the deed by fourteen months, dying at Rome on 22 September 1774 after weeks of wasting illness. That the Jesuits had poisoned him was the whisper of all Europe; no evidence has ever sustained it. He was buried in the church of the Twelve Apostles, and the order he had cut down lay in its grave until Pius VII raised it up again in 1814.

title: The Concordat of Worms
shortBlurb: At Worms, pope and emperor traded ring and sceptre for peace, closing the half-century Investiture Contest…
body: The struggle begun when Gregory VII forbade lay investiture in 1075 had outlived that pope and the emperor he humbled at Canossa. On 23 September 1122, at Worms on the Rhine, Pope Callixtus II and the Emperor Henry V set their names to the two declarations — the first concordat between the Church and a temporal power — that ended it.

The emperor renounced investiture with ring and crosier, the bestowal of spiritual office by a lay hand, and granted that elections should be canonical and consecration free. The pope conceded that in Germany elections might be held in the emperor's presence, and that the elect should receive the regalia by the touch of the sceptre — in Germany before consecration, in Burgundy and Italy within six months after.

The First Lateran Council ratified the concordat the following March. Its distinction of the spiritual sword from the temporal became the pattern of every later settlement between altar and throne, and the Church had won, at parchment's length, the freedom of her bishops.

title: The Second Council of Nicaea opens
shortBlurb: Bishops gathered by the Empress Irene opened at Nicaea the seventh and last council both East and West receive, to judge the veneration of images…
body: Sixty years of iconoclasm had divided the Eastern churches when the Empress Irene, regent for her son Constantine VI, and the Patriarch Tarasius summoned a general council — with the blessing of Pope Hadrian I, whose two legates would sign first among its acts. A first attempt at Constantinople in August 786 was scattered by iconoclast soldiers; the fathers were bidden instead to Nicaea, where the first council had sat.

On 24 September 787, in the church of Hagia Sophia there, some three hundred bishops opened the sessions. The assembly of Hieria, which had proscribed the images in 754, was condemned, and the council defined its measure with care: icons are to receive salutation and honorable reverence — never the worship that belongs to God alone.

The last session was held in the Magnaura palace at Constantinople on 23 October. Christendom reckons Nicaea II its Seventh Ecumenical Council, the last received by East and West alike — though a bungled Latin rendering of its decrees moved the scholars of Charlemagne to protest in the Libri Carolini, and such unity was never again so near.

title: The Peace of Augsburg
shortBlurb: The settlement Ferdinand concluded at Augsburg in his brother's name gave Lutheran princes legal standing — and the Empire sixty-three years of peace…
body: After a generation of religious strife, the diet that opened at Augsburg in February 1555 met an absent emperor: Charles V, spent, had left its conduct to his brother Ferdinand, King of the Romans. On 25 September the peace was published in the emperor's name with the princes of the Augsburg Confession.

Its rule was cuius regio, eius religio: the prince's faith, Catholic or the Lutheranism of Augsburg, should be the faith of his territory, the dissenter free to sell his goods and depart. At Ferdinand's insistence the reservatum ecclesiasticum guarded the lands of any prince-bishop who should turn Protestant, a clause the Protestant estates never accepted; Calvinism and the sects stood outside the peace altogether.

Within weeks Charles resigned the Netherlands and Spain, and the imperial crown followed. The settlement the old emperor had shunned to sign held the German peace for sixty-three years — until a defenestration at Prague in 1618 opened the Thirty Years' War and taught Europe how much the peace of Augsburg had left undone.

title: The battle of the Maritsa
shortBlurb: In a night attack on the Maritsa the Ottomans destroyed the army of the Serbian lords, and the Balkans lay open before them…
body: Since Adrianople had fallen to them about 1361, the Ottoman Turks had pressed into the Balkans. In 1371 the despot Jovan Uglješa and his brother Vukašin, king of Prilep — the two greatest lords of the crumbling Serbian empire of Dušan — gathered a host the chronicles swell to seventy thousand and marched to drive them from Europe.

The Ottoman commander Lala Şahin Pasha had a fraction of their numbers. On the night of 26 September 1371, by the river Maritsa near the village of Chernomen, his men fell upon the Christian camp as it feasted, and the rout was utter: both brothers died on the field, and the victors named the battle Sırp Sındığı, the destruction of the Serbs.

Macedonia and the southern Balkans lay open. Within the year the last Nemanjić emperor, Uroš V, died childless; the Emperor John V of Constantinople became the sultan's tributary; and the road ran on through Kosovo in 1389 and Nicopolis in 1396 to the fall of the imperial city itself in 1453.

title: The death of Pope John Paul I
shortBlurb: Albino Luciani, the smiling pope of thirty-three days, died in the night in the Apostolic Palace, and 1978 became the year of three popes…
body: Albino Luciani, born in 1912 at Forno di Canale in the Veneto, had been bishop of Vittorio Veneto and then patriarch of Venice before the conclave of 26 August 1978 elected him pope. He was the first to join two names — John Paul, for the two popes he honored — and the first to refuse the tiara, taking a simple inauguration on 3 September.

In the night of 28 September, thirty-three days after his election, he died suddenly in his apartment in the Apostolic Palace; he was found lifeless in his bed at first light of the 29th, and the Holy See reckons his death to the 28th. The medical reconstruction concludes an acute myocardial infarction, and the conspiracy theories that flourished in the absence of an autopsy have collapsed under the evidence since published.

The world mourned 'the smiling pope' and laid him in the Vatican grottoes; in October the cardinals gave the Church John Paul II. His cause advanced quietly, and on 4 September 2022 Pope Francis beatified him in St. Peter's Square.

title: Frederick II is excommunicated
shortBlurb: Gregory IX put the ban of the Church on the emperor who would not sail — who then won Jerusalem back while excommunicate…
body: Frederick II, the Hohenstaufen wonder of the world, had vowed at his imperial coronation in 1220 to lead a crusade, and at San Germano in 1225 had sworn it again, this time under penalty of excommunication. When at last he embarked at Brindisi in the September of 1227, only to put back within days with sickness raging in the fleet, Gregory IX would hear no excuses.

On 29 September 1227 the pope pronounced him excommunicate. The sentence did not hold him: on 18 June 1228 Frederick sailed for the East under the ban, and by treaty with the Sultan al-Kamil, concluded at Jaffa in February 1229, he recovered Jerusalem, Bethlehem, and Nazareth without striking a blow — taking the crown of Jerusalem in the church of the Holy Sepulchre on 18 March, in a city lying under interdict.

Reconciled with the pope in 1230, he warred with the papacy on and off for the rest of his reign, was excommunicated again, and was deposed at the Council of Lyons in 1245. He died in 1250, and the chroniclers could not decide whether to mourn a persecutor of the Church or a wonder of the world.
